blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's statement (26 March 2026) on the national parliament's 2026 amendment to the transgender-rights law: it removes self-identification, limits recognition to the country's traditional third-gender-community and intersex categories, mandates medical certification, and creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' someone to be transgender. The research found no divergent statute here, so this national framework — not any local law — defines this state/province's position for visitors.

A national broadcaster's report (26 March 2026): both houses passed the amendment scrapping self-identification and requiring medical-board certification, amid protests; a supreme-court-appointed panel sought withdrawal and presidential assent is pending. The law applies nationally, including in this state/province; no regional coverage, consistent with the research finding of no local divergence in trans law or enforcement.

A national newspaper's city report (18 August 2024): a trans woman alleged a railway-security constable groped her during a 'gender check' at a metro station; authorities denied it and filed a counter-complaint. An incident from a different state/province, not about this one, held as a national datapoint on police and security screening behaviour toward gender-nonconforming people in public spaces — relevant wherever comparable checkpoints exist.
